items.prompt: What is a particle?

options.text: a small stone you can hold
options.why: A stone is made of many, many particles.

options.text: a very tiny piece of a substance
a drop of water
options.why: A drop of water contains millions of particles.

hints: Particles are far too small to see.
Everything is made of them.
It is not something you can hold in your hand.
items.explanation: A particle is a tiny piece of a substance. We cannot see single particles.

items.prompt: Which state of matter has particles that can only vibrate in fixed places?

options.text: liquid
options.why: Liquid particles move past each other.

options.text: solid
gas
options.why: Gas particles move freely.

hints: This state keeps its shape.
Think about a rock or a coin.
The particles do not move from place to place.
items.explanation: In a solid the particles vibrate but stay in fixed places.

items.prompt: In a gas, the particles are far ___.
hints: Think about how much space there is between the particles.
The opposite of close together.
The word starts with a.
items.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, which is why a gas fills all the space it can.

items.prompt: Why can a liquid be poured?

options.text: Its particles are locked in a pattern.
options.why: That describes a solid.

options.text: Its particles can slide past each other.
Its particles are very far apart.
options.why: That describes a gas.

hints: Pouring means the substance flows.
Flowing needs particles that can move.
Liquid particles touch but are not fixed.
items.explanation: Liquid particles are close but free to slide past each other, so a liquid flows.

items.prompt: Why does a gas spread out to fill a whole room?

options.text: Its particles are packed in a fixed pattern.
options.why: Gas particles are not in a pattern.

options.text: Its particles move quickly in all directions and are far apart.
Its particles stick to the walls.
options.why: Gas particles do not stick to the walls.

hints: Think about how gas particles move.
Nothing holds gas particles in place.
They keep moving until they are everywhere.
items.explanation: Gas particles move fast in all directions with nothing to stop them, so they spread out.

items.prompt: Why does a solid keep its shape?

options.text: Its particles have stopped moving.
options.why: Solid particles still vibrate.

options.text: Its particles are held in fixed places.
Its particles are far apart.
options.why: Solid particles are packed close together.

hints: Think about the arrangement of particles in a solid.
They are packed tightly.
They are not free to move around.
items.explanation: Particles in a solid are held in fixed places, so the solid keeps its shape.

items.prompt: The particles in a solid can only ___ in their places.
hints: Solid particles do not move from place to place.
They move a tiny bit back and forth.
The word starts with v.
items.explanation: Solid particles vibrate on the spot.

items.prompt: Sort each description into solid, liquid or gas.
hints: Solids keep their shape.
Liquids flow but stay close together.
Gases spread out as far as they can.
items.explanation: Solids keep their shape, liquids flow, and gases fill their container.

items.prompt: How are the particles in a liquid arranged compared with a solid?

options.text: They are far apart.
options.why: That describes a gas.

options.text: They are close together but not in a fixed pattern.
They are in the same pattern as a solid.
options.why: A solid has a regular pattern, a liquid does not.

hints: A liquid is not a gas, so the particles still touch.
A liquid is not a solid, so there is no fixed pattern.
Think of marbles tumbling in a bag.
items.explanation: Liquid particles are close together but can move around, so they have no fixed pattern.

items.prompt: A gas can be squashed into a smaller space but a solid cannot. Why?

options.text: Gas particles are softer than solid particles.
options.why: Particles are not soft or hard.

options.text: There are large gaps between gas particles.
Gas particles stop moving when squashed.
options.why: Gas particles keep moving.

hints: Think about the space between the particles.
Squashing pushes particles closer together.
Solid particles already touch.
items.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, so there is space to push them closer. Solid particles already touch.

items.prompt: Which statements about particles are true?

options.text: Particles are too small to see with our eyes.
Particles in a solid do not move at all.
options.why: Solid particles vibrate.

options.text: Particles in a gas touch each other all the time.
options.why: Gas particles are far apart.

options.text: Particles are always moving.

hints: Think about the vibrating particles in a solid.
Think about how big particles are.
Gas particles have lots of space.
items.explanation: Particles are tiny and are always moving, even in a solid where they vibrate.

items.prompt: A cup of fine sand can be poured, but each grain of sand is still a solid. What is the best reason?

options.text: Sand particles are really liquid particles.
options.why: Sand is a solid, not a liquid.

options.text: Each tiny grain is a solid, and the grains slide over each other.
The particles in sand are far apart like a gas.
options.why: The particles inside each grain are packed close together.

hints: Look closely at what the grains are made of.
Each grain keeps its own shape.
The pile flows because the grains slide.
items.explanation: Powders pour because many small solid grains slide over each other. Each grain is still a solid.

items.prompt: Particles in a ___ are far apart and move quickly in all directions.
hints: This state fills its container.
It is not a solid or a liquid.
The word has three letters.
items.explanation: Gas particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

items.prompt: Which of these is made of particles?

options.text: only solids
options.why: Liquids and gases are made of particles too.

options.text: everything, including air, water and rock
only things we can see
options.why: Air is made of particles and we cannot see it.

hints: Think about all the states of matter.
The particle model applies to solids, liquids and gases.
Air is matter too.
items.explanation: All matter is made of particles, including gases that we cannot see.

items.prompt: You push the plunger of a sealed syringe full of air. Why can the air be squashed?

options.text: The air particles get smaller.
options.why: Particles do not change size when squashed.

options.text: The air particles move closer together because there are gaps between them.
The air particles disappear.
options.why: Particles are not lost. They are pushed closer.

hints: What changes when the air takes up less space?
Think about the gaps in a gas.
The same number of particles are still there.
items.explanation: There is a lot of space between gas particles, so pushing the plunger moves them closer together.

items.prompt: A student heats a solid and the particles vibrate more. What do you expect if it is heated a lot?

options.text: The particles stop moving.
options.why: Heating makes particles move more, not less.

options.text: The particles may break free of their places and the solid can melt.
The particles get bigger and stay in place.
options.why: Particles do not grow. They move more.

hints: More energy makes particles move more.
What happens when a solid melts?
Think of ice turning into water.
items.explanation: More heat makes particles vibrate more. If they break free of their places, the solid melts into a liquid.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to say that one particle of water is wet?

options.text: Water particles are always dry.
options.why: The idea of wet or dry applies to a large amount of water.

options.text: Wetness is a property of lots of particles together.
A particle is too big to be wet.
options.why: A particle is far too small, not too big.

hints: Think about properties like wet, hot and hard.
They describe materials, not one particle.
A single particle is far too small to feel.
items.explanation: Properties such as wet or hard describe a material made of huge numbers of particles, not a single particle.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a material and a particle?

options.text: A particle is made of huge numbers of materials.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: A material is made of huge numbers of particles.
They mean the same thing.
options.why: They are different. A material is something we can handle and see.

hints: Which one can you hold?
Which one is far too small to see?
Think of a spoon of sugar.
items.explanation: A material, such as sugar, is made of an enormous number of tiny particles.

items.prompt: You can smell perfume from across a room. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Air particles carry the smell because they are bigger.
options.why: Air particles are not bigger than perfume particles.

options.text: Perfume particles move about among the air particles and spread out.
Perfume particles are lighter than air so they float to you.
options.why: The smell spreads because the particles keep moving, not because they float.

hints: Gas particles are always moving.
They spread out to fill the room.
Think about the gaps between air particles.
items.explanation: Perfume particles keep moving and mix with the air particles, so the smell spreads through the room.

items.prompt: A powder pours like a liquid. Which statement is true?

options.text: It is a liquid because it flows.
options.why: Flowing alone does not make it a liquid. Each grain keeps its shape.

options.text: It is a solid made of lots of tiny grains.
It is a gas because it spreads out.
options.why: A powder does not spread through the air like a gas.

hints: Does each grain keep its own shape?
A pile of grains can slide.
Look at one grain, not the whole pile.
items.explanation: Each grain is a solid with fixed shape. The pile flows because the grains slide over each other.

items.prompt: Put the states in order from the particles that are closest together to the particles that are furthest apart.
hints: Solids have the tightest packing.
Liquids are a little looser.
Gas particles have the most space.
items.explanation: Solid particles are packed tightest, liquid particles are close but loose, and gas particles are furthest apart.

items.prompt: Which statements describe particles in a liquid?

options.text: They are very far apart.
options.why: That describes a gas.

options.text: They are close together.
They can slide past each other.
They are held in a fixed pattern.
options.why: That describes a solid.

hints: A liquid is not a solid.
A liquid is not a gas.
Particles in a liquid touch and move.
items.explanation: Liquid particles are close together but can slide past each other.

items.prompt: True or false: The particles in a solid are packed closely together.

options.text: True
False

hints: Are particles loose in a solid?
Solids are hard.
They are packed tight.
items.explanation: They are held in a regular pattern, so a solid holds its shape.

items.prompt: True or false: The particles in a gas are close together and cannot move.

options.text: True
False

hints: Does a gas stay in one place?
Gas spreads out.
They are far apart.
items.explanation: Gas particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, which is why gases spread out.

items.prompt: True or false: The particles in a liquid can slide past each other.

options.text: True
False

hints: Does a liquid flow?
Particles move around.
Liquids flow.
items.explanation: They are close but not fixed, which is why a liquid flows.

items.prompt: True or false: When a solid melts, its particles stop moving.

options.text: True
False

hints: Does heat add energy?
More energy means more movement.
They move more.
items.explanation: Heating makes particles move more. In melting they gain enough energy to slide past each other.
